standard_text: Counting amounts of money in cents up to $1 and in dollars up to $100
meta_desc: Free P1 money practice: name Singapore coins and notes, count cents up to $1 and dollars up to $100, compare and buy. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Count the value of each coin or note, not how many there are.
body_html:
Singapore coins and notes

Coins are round. Notes are paper money. Each one shows its value. The ¢ sign means cents. The $ sign means dollars.

We writeWe say
20¢twenty cents
$1one dollar = 100¢
$5five dollars
$50fifty dollars

Count coins in cents

Start with the coin worth the most. Count on with each coin. Write ¢ after the number.

Example

How much are three 20¢ coins?

Count by 20s: 20¢, 40¢, 60¢.

Answer: 60¢

Count notes in dollars

Count notes the same way. Write $ before the number.

Example

Siti buys a book for $6. She pays with a $10 note. What is her change?

$10 − $6 = $4.

Answer: $4

Which is more?

Look at the value, not the number of coins. One 50¢ coin is more than four 5¢ coins.

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Three 10¢ coins, so 3¢Count the value: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢
Writing 30¢ as $30Coins under $1 are cents. Write 30¢
50¢ is more than $5$5 is dollars. Cents are worth less than $1
More coins is more moneyFour 5¢ coins (20¢) are less than one 50¢ coin

faq.q: What do Primary 1 students learn about money?
faq.a: In Primary 1, students name Singapore coins and notes, count coins in cents up to $1, and count notes in dollars up to $100. They also compare amounts and solve simple buying problems.

faq.q: How can I help my child count money at home?
faq.a: Use real coins and notes. Sort them, then count on from the one worth the most, such as 50¢, 70¢, 80¢. Let your child pay for a small snack and check the change.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake with money in P1?
faq.a: Counting the coins instead of their value, so three 10¢ coins become 3¢. Many children also mix up cents and dollars, writing 30¢ as $30.

faq.q: Is money in the MOE Primary 1 syllabus?
faq.a: Yes. Money is part of Number and Algebra in the MOE 2021 Primary Mathematics Syllabus for Primary 1. Amounts like $1.20 with dollars and cents together come in Primary 2.

items.q: What is this?
items.e: It says 20¢. The ¢ sign means cents. It is a 20¢ coin.

items.q: What is this?
items.e: It says 50¢. It is a 50¢ coin. A $50 note is worth much more.

items.q: What is this?

items.q: What is this?
items.e: It says $10. The $ sign means dollars. It is a $10 note.

items.q: Which one is the $5 note?
items.e: The $5 note says $5. It is B. 5¢ and 50¢ are coins.

items.q: Which one is the 10¢ coin?
items.e: The 10¢ coin says 10¢. It is D. $10 is a note.

items.q: Which one is the $1 coin?
items.e: The $1 coin says $1. It is A.

items.q: Which one is the 50¢ coin?
items.e: The 50¢ coin says 50¢. It is A. $50 is a note.

items.q: Which one is the $50 note?
items.e: The $50 note says $50. It is C.

items.q: How many coins are there?
items.e: Coins are round. Count only the round ones: 5 coins. 7 counts the notes too.

items.q: How many notes are there?
items.e: Notes are paper money. They are long. There are 3 notes: $10, $2 and $50. The $1 is a coin.

items.q: Which one is a note?
items.e: The $2 is a note. The $1 is a coin, not a note.

items.q: Which coin is the smallest?
items.e: The 5¢ coin is the smallest. It is also worth the least.

items.q: Which coin is worth the most?
items.e: $1 is 100¢. That is more than 50¢. The $1 coin is worth the most.

items.q: Which note is worth the most?
items.e: 50 is the biggest number. The $50 note is worth the most.

items.q: How do we say 20¢?
items.e: The ¢ sign means cents. 20¢ is twenty cents.

items.q: How do we say $50?
items.e: The $ sign means dollars. $50 is fifty dollars.

items.q: How many cents make $1?
items.e: $1 is the same as 100¢. Two 50¢ coins also make $1.

items.q: How do we write ten cents?
items.e: Write the number, then the ¢ sign: 10¢. $10 is ten dollars.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each one is 10¢. Count by 10s: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢. That is 30¢. 3¢ counts the coins, not the cents. $30 is dollars. Coins under $1 are cents (¢).

items.q: Ryan has these coins. How much does he have?
items.e: Each one is 5¢. Count by 5s: 5¢, 10¢, 15¢, 20¢. That is 20¢. 4¢ counts the coins, not the cents. $20 is dollars. Coins under $1 are cents (¢).

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Each one is 20¢. Count by 20s: 20¢, 40¢, 60¢. That is 60¢. 3¢ counts the coins, not the cents. $60 is dollars. Coins under $1 are cents (¢).

items.e: 10¢, 20¢, 30¢, 40¢, 50¢. Five 10¢ coins make 50¢. Five 5¢ coins make only 25¢.

items.q: How much money is this?
items.e: Each one is $2. Count by 2s: $2, $4, $6. That is $6. $3 counts the notes, not the dollars. Notes are dollars ($), not cents (¢).

items.q: Priya has these notes. How much does she have?
items.e: Each one is $5. Count by 5s: $5, $10, $15, $20. That is $20. $4 counts the notes, not the dollars. Notes are dollars ($), not cents (¢).

items.q: What is the total?
items.e: Each one is $10. Count by 10s: $10, $20, $30, $40, $50. That is $50. $5 counts the notes, not the dollars. Notes are dollars ($), not cents (¢).

items.q: Hafiz keeps these notes in his wallet. How much is it?

items.q: Count by 5s. What comes next?
items.e: Count by 5s: $5, $10, $15, $20. $16 counts by 1s.

items.q: How many $10 notes make $50?
items.e: Count by 10s: $10, $20, $30, $40, $50. That is 5 notes.

items.q: How many $5 notes make $10?
items.e: $5 + $5 = $10. That is 2 notes.

items.q: How many $2 notes make $10?
items.e: Count by 2s: $2, $4, $6, $8, $10. That is 5 notes.

items.q: Which is worth more?
items.e: 50¢ is more than 20¢. So the 50¢ coin is worth more.

items.q: Which is worth more?
items.e: 10¢ is more than 5¢. So the 10¢ coin is worth more.

items.q: Which is worth more?
items.e: $1 is more than 50¢. So the $1 coin is worth more. $1 is 100¢.

items.q: Which is worth more?
items.e: $2 is more than $1. So the $2 note is worth more.

items.q: Which is worth more?
items.e: $5 is more than 50¢. So the $5 note is worth more. 50 is a bigger number, but 50¢ is cents. $5 is dollars.

items.q: Which is worth less?
items.e: $5 is less than $10. So the $5 note is worth less.

items.q: Which is worth less?
items.e: 20¢ is less than $2. So the 20¢ coin is worth less. Cents are worth less than dollars.

items.q: Which is worth less?
items.e: $10 is less than $50. So the $10 note is worth less.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: Four 5¢ coins make 20¢. One 50¢ coin is 50¢. So the 50¢ coin is worth more. More coins or notes is not always more money.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: Five 10¢ coins make 50¢. One 50¢ coin is 50¢. They are the same.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: Three 20¢ coins make 60¢. One 50¢ coin is 50¢. So the three 20¢ coins are worth more.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: One $10 note is $10. Two $5 notes make $10. They are the same.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: Three $2 notes make $6. One $5 note is $5. So the three $2 notes are worth more.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: Four $2 notes make $8. One $10 note is $10. So the $10 note is worth more. More coins or notes is not always more money.

items.q: Which side is worth more?
items.e: One $50 note is $50. Six $5 notes make $30. So the $50 note is worth more. More coins or notes is not always more money.

items.q: Which costs more?
items.e: $1 is 100¢. 100¢ is more than 80¢. So the snack costs more. Do not just compare 80 and 1.

items.q: Which costs less?
items.e: 90¢ is less than $1. $9 is nine dollars. So the drink costs less.

items.q: Which costs more?
items.e: $1 is the same as 100¢. They are the same. 100 is a big number, but it is cents.

items.q: Which is worth the most?
items.e: In order: 20¢, 50¢, $2, $5. The $5 note is worth the most.

items.q: Which is worth the least?
items.e: In order: 50¢, $1, $2, $10. The 50¢ coin is worth the least. 50¢ is less than $1.

items.q: A packet of milk costs 60¢. Arjun has these coins. Is it enough?
items.e: 50¢, 60¢. Arjun has 60¢. Yes, it is enough. 2¢ counts the coins.

items.q: A bun costs 50¢. Hui Min has these coins. Is it enough?
items.e: 20¢, 40¢. Hui Min has 40¢. 40¢ + 10¢ = 50¢. She needs 10¢ more.

items.q: Ahmad buys a bun and a drink. How much does he spend?
items.e: 60¢ + 30¢ = 90¢. 30¢ takes away instead of adding.

items.q: Jun Jie has 80¢. He buys biscuits for 50¢. How much is left?
items.e: 80¢ − 50¢ = 30¢. 50¢ is the price, not what is left.

items.q: Zhi Hao has $5. He buys a toy car for $3. How much is left?
items.e: $5 − $3 = $2. $8 adds instead of taking away.

items.q: Raju pays for this book with a $10 note. What is his change?
items.e: $10 − $7 = $3. $7 is the price, not the change.

items.q: At the hawker centre, Devi buys both. How much is that?
items.e: $4 + $2 = $6. $2 takes away instead of adding.

items.q: Which two coins pay exactly 70¢?
A sweet costs 20¢. Which one pays exactly?
items.e: The 20¢ coin pays exactly 20¢. It is C. The $2 note is dollars, not cents.

items.q: A book costs $5. Which one pays exactly?
items.e: The $5 note pays exactly $5. It is C. 5¢ and 50¢ are cents.

items.q: Priya has these coins. A drink costs 50¢. Can she buy it?
items.e: Count by 20s: 20¢, 40¢, 60¢. 60¢ is more than 50¢, so yes. 30¢ counts by 10s.

items.q: Ali saves a $2 note each week for 4 weeks. How much?
items.e: Count by 2s: $2, $4, $6, $8. That is $8. $4 counts the notes.

items.q: At Chinese New Year, Hafiz gets these in red packets. How much?
items.e: $10, $15, $17. That is $17. $3 counts the notes.

items.q: An ice cream costs $1. Chloe has these coins. How much more does she need?
items.e: 50¢, 70¢, 90¢. Chloe has 90¢. $1 is 100¢. 90¢ + 10¢ = 100¢. She needs 10¢ more. 90¢ is what she has.

items.q: Mei Ling buys 2 packets of milk. How much is that?
items.e: 40¢ + 40¢ = 80¢. 40¢ is the price of only 1 packet.

items.q: A book at the book fair costs $9. Xin Yi has these notes. Is it enough?
items.e: $5, $7, $9. Xin Yi has $9. Yes, it is enough. $3 counts the notes.

items.q: Ryan looks at the canteen. Which costs more?
items.e: 90¢ is less than $1. $2 is more than $1. So the sandwich costs more. Do not compare 90 and 2.

items.q: Mrs Lim buys mandarin oranges for $20. How many $10 notes does she pay?
items.e: $10, $20. That is 2 notes. 20 is the dollars, not the notes.

items.q: Siti has these coins. She buys a 75¢ snack. How much is left?
Kavya buys both. She pays with a $10 note. What is the change?
items.e: $5 + $3 = $8. $10 − $8 = $2. $8 is the cost, not the change.
